newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Future HK chief must perform tricky balancing act.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Future HK chief must perform tricky balancing act.

text.p: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's future leader, has no political track record, no role model and no historical precedent to guide him. Just winks and nudges from China's Communist rulers, plus his own conservative intuitions.
For the spiky grey-haired tycoon who wears grey pinstriped suits, it's a uniquely tough job at a crssroads of history, requiring a tightrope walker's sense of balance.
Tung, a former shipping magnate, is to become Hong Kong's first Chief Executive, succeeding Governor Chris Patten when Britain hands the colony back to China at midnight on June 30.

Tung will steer the territory of 6.4 million people -- the eighth largest trading economy, with the world's highest per capita ownership of Rolls Royce cars -- into the fold of communist China after 156 years under colonial rule.
IN FIRING LINE OF DEMOCRATS, TUNG PURSUES OWN VISION

In the firing line of angry democrats who see him as the puppet of an authoritarian Beijing, Tung noted recently that life at the top for him is a lonely affair but he has vowed to defend Hong Kong's best interests and pursue his own vision.
That vision is a society where capitalism will have free rein but where traditional Chinese values will be resurrected and more attention paid to housing, education and welfare.
"I want the Hong Kong we take into the 21st century to remain stable, harmonious, free and vibrant. To do this we must accord high priority to livelihood issues," he said.

"We need to renew our commitment to the traditional virtues of modesty, hard work...emphasis on obligations rather than individual rights and the willingness to sacrifice one's interest for the common good."
Born in Shanghai in 1937 and educated at Britain's Liverpool University, Tung was chosen last December by a China-controlled committee to govern Hong Kong.
Only six months ago, Tung, who turns 60 on May 29, was a reclusive shipping billionaire who kept his political views to himself, balancing loyalties to China and Britain.
But in a short time he has evolved into a conservative Chinese patriot, loudly singing China's tune on key issues.

He has launched a plan to trim back political liberties, ban foreign funding of political groups and limit protest rights. He has also appointed his inner cabinet, the Executive Council, with a line-up dominated by pro-China corporate bosses.
"I lived in America in the 1960s and I saw how society became less orderly than desirable. I don't want that to happen here," he told reporters.

The ban on foreign funding appeared hypocritical to many, when Tung acknowledged recently he had personally donated 50,000 pounds sterling (about $75,000) to the then-ruling British Conservative Party in 1992.
Tung's problem is that he is untested as a politician, and the people of Hong Kong have only his word to go by.
NO TIANANMEN CRACKDOWNS IN HONG KONG
He says his China-inspired moves against civil liberties do not augur crackdowns like China's bloody suppression of student pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
"We live in a different world...It cannot happen here. It will not happen here. I will not allow it to happen here," Tung said in a television interview.

The change of civil rights laws will not mean an end to the freedom of assembly, he said. But he has said defaming Chinese leaders and staging demonstrations to press for the independence of Hong Kong, Taiwan or Tibet will not be allowed.
Tung sparked anxiety by attacking the head of the Democratic Party, Martin Lee, for "badmouthing" Hong Kong abroad.

Tung is trying to make sure Hong Kong remains a freewheeling city and economic miracle, while preventing it from being a centre of anti-China political forces that would provoke Beijing into a crackdown.
RELATIONS SOUR WITH DEPARTING COLONIALS
Relations between Tung and the British authorities are so sour that he and Patten avoid meeting at cocktail parties.
Tung is not without his admirers abroad, however.

"Politicians in Hong Kong, the United States and elsewhere need to focus on the agreements China has pledged to honour and rally behind Mr Tung, the man with the heavy responsibility, both of keeping Beijing happy and protecting the freedom and prosperity of his people," said Ralph Cossa, executive director of the Pacific Forum foreign policy research institute.
Tung is privately soft spoken and polite, described by friends as a traditional gentleman.

He lives with his wife Betty in a large apartment in the trendy Mid-Levels area, and his family owns a Chinese style mansion on the south side of Hong Kong Island with its own cinema, karaoke lounge and pool.
He gave up a job in the United States and returned to Hong Kong to be eased into the hotseat of his family's shipping empire, taking over from his father C.Y. Tung, who died in 1982.

He has publicly acknowledged China helped engineer a US$120 million bailout when the company floundered 11 years ago. Tung resigned from Patten's advisory cabinet in June 1996 and then as head of the Orient Overseas (International) business last October to compete for the Hong Kong leadership.
